experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/a: Paraphrase with short quotation from Revelations of Divine Love (Long Text): at thirty and a half years old, on 8 or 13 May 1373, gravely ill and given the last rites, Julian gazes at a crucifix and receives sixteen 'showings' over a night and day: the bleeding head of Christ, a hazelnut-sized thing representing 'all that is made', and Christ telling her that sin is 'behovely' and that 'all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' (ch. 27). She recovers, and spends some twenty years reflecting on their meaning, including Christ as Mother.
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/c: Julian lived as an anchoress at St Julian's church, Norwich. Margery Kempe records consulting her about discernment of her own visions (c. 1413), and Julian advised testing whether they led to charity and conformity with the faith.
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/a: Venerated (her feast is kept locally) and widely read; her optimism about divine love is admired, while some theologians ask how her near-universal hope fits Church teaching on judgement.
Commemorated on 8 May in the Church of England; often treated as a mother of English spiritual writing.
Appreciated for devotion to the cross; some critics question the 'Christ as Mother' imagery and hints of universalism.
Her texts are well documented (manuscripts c. 15th-17th c.); the Short Text may date from the 1380s, the Long from the 1390s-1410s. Her illness-and-recovery narrative is plausibly autobiographical.
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/d: Universal salvation hints ('all shall be well').
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/s:
Norwich in the late fourteenth century was one of the largest and richest cities in England, a centre of the wool trade with dozens of parish churches, a cathedral priory and many religious houses. It was also a place of suffering: the Black Death had struck in 1348-1349 and returned several times; the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was put down harshly by Bishop Henry Despenser; and from the 1390s Lollards, followers of John Wycliffe, were tried and later burned at the Lollards' Pit just outside the city. Against this background a woman whose own name is unknown wrote the earliest surviving book in English known to be by a woman.

We know her as Julian because she later lived as an anchoress, enclosed in a cell attached to the church of St Julian at Conisford in Norwich. Almost all information comes from her own book, known as Revelations of Divine Love or the Showings. She says that as a young woman she had asked God for three gifts: a vivid understanding of Christ's passion, a bodily sickness bringing her close to death, and three 'wounds' of contrition, compassion and longing for God.

In May 1373, when she was thirty and a half years old (the date is given as 8 May in most manuscripts, 13 May in one), she fell gravely ill. After several days she was believed to be dying, and the last rites were given. A curate set a crucifix before her face and told her to look on it. As she gazed at it, she writes, her pain suddenly left her and she began to see the crucified Christ bleeding, the blood running down from under the crown of thorns, so vividly that it seemed alive. Over that day and the following night she received sixteen 'showings', some seen 'bodily', some as words formed in her understanding, and some as 'spiritual sight'.

Among the best known is the vision of a little thing, the size of a hazelnut, lying in the palm of her hand, round as a ball. She asked what it could be and was answered that it was 'all that is made'; she marvelled that it could last, and understood that it lasts and always will because God loves it. She saw that God made it, loves it and keeps it. She also wrestled with the problem of sin: why, she asked, had God not prevented it? The answer she reports became the most quoted line of her book: "Sin is behovely, but all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." (behovely: necessary or fitting)

After the visions she briefly doubted them, telling a visiting priest that she had raved; she was ashamed of the denial, and a final showing confirmed her. She recovered. She wrote down a shorter account (the Short Text), probably soon after, and then, after some twenty years of reflection, a much longer version (the Long Text) with extended theological commentary. There she developed a distinctive theology: God sees in us no wrath; sin is real but cannot finally defeat divine love; and Christ is our mother, who bears us, feeds us with himself and cares for us with a mother's tenderness, an image with roots in Anselm and earlier writers that she made central.

By the early fifteenth century Julian was a respected spiritual counsellor. Margery Kempe, the mystic of King's Lynn, records visiting her around 1413 and receiving advice about discerning her own experiences. Wills mention bequests to Julian between 1393 and 1416, after which she disappears from the record. Her book survived in only a few manuscripts, mainly copied by English Benedictine nuns in exile in France after the Reformation; it was first printed in 1670 by the Benedictine Serenus Cressy.

Julian's book has been read widely since the early twentieth century. Some theologians ask whether her 'all shall be well' implies universal salvation; she herself affirms the Church's teaching about hell while confessing she could not see how her vision fitted with it, leaving the tension unresolved.
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/k: Julian is born, to judge from her own statement of her age in 1373; her birthplace and original name are unknown.
Aged thirty and a half and believed to be dying, she gazes on a crucifix and begins to receive sixteen 'showings'.
She recovers, briefly doubts the visions, and then writes the Short Text of her Revelations.
Julian is recorded as an anchoress at St Julian's Church, Conisford, Norwich, in a will bequest.
After about twenty years of reflection she completes the Long Text, developing themes such as Christ as mother.
Margery Kempe visits Julian for counsel about her own spiritual experiences.
The last known bequest to Julian is recorded; she probably died soon after.
Serenus Cressy publishes the first printed edition of the Revelations.
experiences/julian-of-norwich-showings/s: Julian's Revelations is the earliest surviving book in English known to be written by a woman and one of the most influential works of English spirituality. Her optimism about divine love in the face of sin and suffering, her image of Christ as mother and her careful theology of experience have made her popular across Anglican, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers, and she is commemorated on 8 May in Anglican and Lutheran calendars. Theologians debate whether her vision implies universal salvation and how it relates to Augustinian teaching on sin and judgment. She has also become a key figure in feminist theology and in modern contemplative movements, readings that some historians caution can obscure her late medieval context.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/titl: Teresa of Ávila: the transverberation and interior castle
experiences/teresa-transverberation/acco: Paraphrase of Teresa's Life (Libro de la vida, ch. 29): she sees beside her a small, very beautiful angel holding a long golden spear with a point of fire, which he seems to thrust several times into her heart; drawing it out, he leaves her wholly on fire with love of God, the pain so great it makes her moan yet the sweetness so excessive she does not wish it to stop. She describes the pain as spiritual, though the body shares in it. She also reports raptures and levitations which embarrassed her, and later maps prayer as seven 'mansions' in The Interior Castle (1577).
experiences/teresa-transverberation/cont: Teresa wrote under obedience to confessors, amid the Spanish Inquisition's suspicion of alumbrados (illuminists) and women visionaries; the Inquisition examined the Life. Several confessors initially told her the visions were demonic. Her reform founded the Discalced Carmelites with John of the Cross.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/asse: Canonised 1622 and the first woman Doctor of the Church (1970); her teaching on prayer is a benchmark of orthodox mysticism. The transverberation is commemorated by the Carmelites (26 August) and Bernini's sculpture in Rome.
Her writings are widely read for prayer; many Protestants question raptures and levitations while valuing her realism, humour and Christ-centredness.
Some charismatics draw parallels between her raptures and Spirit-filled experiences; she herself warned that such favours are not the measure of holiness.

Read in the context of the Inquisition, gender and converso ancestry (her grandfather was a Jewish convert); 20th-century psychiatry speculated about hysteria or epilepsy, interpretations now regarded as reductive.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/deba: Discernment under the Inquisition: illuminism vs. orthodox mysticism.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/stor:
Sixteenth-century Spain was the most powerful Catholic monarchy in Europe, fresh from the conquest of Granada and the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and building an empire in the Americas. The Spanish Inquisition watched closely for heresy, for Protestant influence and for the alumbrados ('illuminated ones'), mystics accused of claiming direct inspiration that bypassed the Church. Women claiming visions were viewed with particular suspicion. In this setting lived Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada, born in Ávila on 28 March 1515. Her paternal grandfather, a converso (a Christian of Jewish descent) from Toledo, had been penalised by the Inquisition in 1485 for returning to Jewish practice, a fact that came to light only in modern research.

Lively, sociable and fond of romances of chivalry, Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Ávila in 1535, against her father's wishes at first. The convent was large and relatively relaxed: nuns received visitors in the parlour and wealthy sisters kept comfortable apartments. Soon after her profession she fell gravely ill, at one point lying in a coma for days and being taken for dead. For nearly twenty years, by her own account in her Life, she struggled half-heartedly with prayer. A decisive change came around 1554 when, moved by an image of the wounded Christ, she gave herself wholly to prayer, and soon after was deeply affected by reading Augustine's Confessions.

From then on she began to experience intense mystical states, locutions (words heard inwardly) and intellectual visions of Christ. Some confessors feared she was deceived by the devil, and one advised her to make a gesture of contempt at her visions, which she did with great distress. Others, including Jesuit confessors and the Franciscan reformer Peter of Alcántara, reassured her.

In chapter 29 of her Life, written in the early 1560s at her confessors' command, Teresa describes the experience that tradition calls the transverberation (the 'piercing through'). She writes that she saw beside her, on her left side, an angel in bodily form, not large but small and very beautiful, his face so aflame that he seemed one of the highest angels. In his hands she saw a long golden spear with what seemed a point of fire at its tip. He seemed to plunge it several times into her heart, reaching her very entrails, and when he drew it out, she felt he drew them with it and left her wholly on fire with a great love of God. The pain, she wrote, was so great that it made her moan, and yet so surpassing was its sweetness that she could not wish to be rid of it; it was not bodily pain but spiritual, though the body had a share in it. The experience, she says, recurred over some days. It is usually dated around 1559-1560.

Teresa interpreted such experiences as calling her to a stricter, more prayerful life. In 1562, with the support of Peter of Alcántara and the bishop of Ávila but against much local opposition, she founded the small convent of St Joseph in Ávila under the primitive Carmelite rule, with enclosure, poverty and the nuns going barefoot or in sandals ('discalced'). Over the next twenty years she founded seventeen convents for women and, with John of the Cross, whom she met in 1567, began the reform among friars. Her Life was examined by the Inquisition, which held the manuscript for years without condemning it. She wrote The Way of Perfection and, in 1577, The Interior Castle, mapping the soul's journey through seven 'mansions' to union with God.

Teresa died on 4 October 1582 at Alba de Tormes. She was canonised in 1622, alongside Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier. Her heart, preserved at Alba de Tormes, was venerated as bearing a wound; the Carmelites obtained a feast of the Transverberation, kept on 26 August. Gian Lorenzo Bernini sculpted the scene as the Ecstasy of St Teresa (1647-1652) in the Cornaro Chapel of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome.

Interpretations have varied. Catholic tradition treats the transverberation as a classic instance of a 'wound of love' in mystical theology. Critics, from some Protestant writers to modern psychoanalysts, have read it in erotic or psychological terms, an interpretation encouraged by Bernini's sensual sculpture. Many scholars point out that Teresa herself carefully distinguished spiritual from bodily experience and wrote under pressure to show her orthodoxy to the Inquisition.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/keyM: Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada is born in Ávila to a family of partly converso descent.
She enters the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation in Ávila.
Moved by an image of the wounded Christ, she commits herself wholeheartedly to prayer and begins to experience mystical graces.
According to her Life, an angel pierces her heart with a fiery golden spear, the experience later called the transverberation.
She founds the reformed convent of St Joseph in Ávila, the first house of the Discalced Carmelites.
Teresa meets John of the Cross at Medina del Campo and enlists him for the reform of the friars.
She writes The Interior Castle, her mature account of the soul's journey to union with God.
Teresa dies at Alba de Tormes; she is canonised in 1622 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
experiences/teresa-transverberation/sign: Teresa of Ávila is one of the most influential mystics and reformers of early modern Catholicism: her Discalced Carmelite reform spread worldwide, and her writings on prayer became standard guides to contemplative life. The transverberation became an iconic image of mystical love, especially through Bernini's sculpture, and shaped Baroque spirituality and art. In 1970 she became one of the first two women named Doctors of the Church. Protestant critics historically regarded such visions as unscriptural enthusiasm, and modern readers have offered psychological and erotic interpretations, while scholars emphasise her careful self-scrutiny under the Inquisition's watch and her remarkable achievement as a woman writer in Counter-Reformation Spain.
